terms.meaning: weighted average cost of capital, the blended rate a business pays to its owners and lenders, used to discount future cash
capital asset pricing model, a formula that estimates the return owners expect from a stock using the risk-free rate, beta and market return
a measure of how much a company's value moves compared with the whole market
discounted cash flow, a valuation method that shrinks future cash back to today's value

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports for the calculation engine
sections.what: Brings in the type-hint helpers, the table tool and the number tool that the calculations rely on. It also states what the module is for.
sections.why: Likely reason: lists and tables are needed throughout the calculations.

sections.name: FinancialCalculator (part 1)
sections.title: Setup, revenue and cost of goods
sections.what: Stores the start year and number of years. Builds yearly revenue from a starting figure and growth rates, then yearly cost of goods sold, gross profit and gross margin from cost percentages.
sections.why: Likely reason: revenue is the starting point, so the other lines are built on top of it. Segment input is accepted but not used in the calculation.
sections.watch_out: The code pairs lists with zip, which silently drops extra items when lists differ in length, so a short list can cut off years without an error.

sections.name: FinancialCalculator: calculate_opex
sections.title: Operating costs and depreciation
sections.what: Works out research and sales costs for each year from percentages. Spreads each year's capital spending evenly over the chosen number of years to get depreciation.
sections.why: Likely reason: even spreading, called straight-line depreciation, is the simplest standard method. The docstring names the method.
sections.watch_out: A depreciation period of zero causes a divide-by-zero error. Spending that falls after the forecast window is not depreciated inside the model.

sections.name: FinancialCalculator: calculate_working_capital
sections.title: Working capital from days
sections.what: Estimates the money tied up in customer bills, stock and supplier bills using days outstanding. Then works out the change in that money from one year to the next.
sections.why: Likely reason: days outstanding is a common way to estimate working capital. The defaults of 45, 60 and 30 days are set in the code.
sections.watch_out: The first year's change is set to zero, so any opening balance is ignored. The sign of the change matters later when it is subtracted in the cash flow.

sections.name: FinancialCalculator: build_three_statements
sections.title: Building the income statement
sections.what: Turns the pieces into the income statement: operating profit before depreciation, depreciation, operating profit, interest on debt, pre-tax profit, tax and net income. Tax is never negative, so losses produce no tax credit.
sections.why: Likely reason: the no-credit rule on losses is the cautious choice and is written directly into the code. Reason not stated otherwise.
sections.watch_out: Interest is the same debt amount times the rate every year, with no repayment, so debt never falls in this model.

sections.name: FinancialCalculator (part 5)
sections.title: Cash flow and simplified balance sheet
sections.what: Builds the cash flow statement with operating cash flow, investing cash flow and free cash flow. Also builds a simplified balance sheet with receivables, inventory, payables, debt and a running total of profit.
sections.why: Likely reason: free cash flow is needed for the valuation. The balance sheet is labelled simplified in the code.
sections.watch_out: The balance sheet is not checked to balance, and retained earnings are only a running sum of profit with no dividends, so treat it as an estimate.

sections.name: FinancialCalculator: calculate_dcf_valuation
sections.title: Discounted cash flow valuation
sections.what: Shrinks each year's free cash flow back to today using the WACC, adds a terminal value for years beyond the forecast, and adds everything to get enterprise value.
sections.why: Likely reason: this is the standard way to put a present value on future cash. The choice to treat each cash flow as arriving at year end is not explained in the code.
sections.watch_out: If the WACC is not above the terminal growth rate, the terminal value formula gives a meaningless or negative number, and nothing in the code prevents this.

sections.name: FinancialCalculator: calculate_wacc
sections.title: Cost of capital calculation
sections.what: Works out the cost of equity with the CAPM method, which is the risk-free rate plus beta times the market premium. Blends that with the after-tax cost of debt, weighted by the share of debt, to get WACC.
sections.why: Likely reason: this is the standard textbook formula for WACC. The docstring names the CAPM method.
sections.watch_out: The debt ratio is not checked to be between zero and one, and the result is only as good as the market inputs supplied to it.

sections.name: DamodaranResearch (part 1)
sections.title: Industry beta and margin lookup tables
sections.what: Holds a small built-in table of typical stock risk (beta) and profit margins for several industries, and returns the matching values for an industry name. Unknown industries get a default beta of 1.0 and a default margin set.
sections.why: Likely reason: the code comments say these are sample values standing in for data that would be pulled from the Damodaran research site later.
sections.watch_out: These are hand-entered sample numbers, not current Damodaran data, and an unknown industry silently receives the defaults.

sections.name: DamodaranResearch: get_market_data
sections.title: Fixed market assumptions for valuation
sections.what: Returns a fixed set of market figures: a 4.2 percent risk-free rate, a 5.8 percent equity risk premium, a 10 percent market return, and a 25 percent default tax rate. The same values come back every time.
sections.why: Likely reason: placeholder values so valuation can run before live market data is connected. Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The comments call these current or historical figures, but nothing updates them, so they can go stale.

sections.name: entry point
sections.title: Simple load check when run directly
sections.what: When the file is run from the command line, it prints a short message confirming the module loaded and naming its two classes. It runs no calculations.
sections.why: Likely reason: a quick check that the file loads without errors.
sections.watch_out: A successful message does not mean the calculations are correct.

summary: Holds the calculations that build revenue, costs, the three financial statements, the cost of capital (WACC) and the discounted cash flow valuation.
purpose: Does the core financial math for the model, so the web routes in app_backend.py only need to call it.
why: Likely reason: keeps all the number work in one place, separate from the web code. The code does not state this directly.
how: 1. Stores the start year and number of years. 2. Builds revenue from a starting figure and growth rates. 3. Builds cost of goods sold, operating costs, and depreciation from percentages and capital spending. 4. Builds working capital from days outstanding. 5. Combines these into the income statement, cash flow statement and a simplified balance sheet. 6. Works out the cost of equity and the WACC. 7. Discounts the free cash flows and adds a terminal value to get enterprise value.
inputs: Starting revenue, growth rates by year, cost percentages by year, capital spending by year, depreciation years, working capital days, tax rate, interest rate, initial debt, beta, terminal growth rate, risk-free rate, market return, debt ratio and cost of debt.
outputs: Tables for revenue, costs, capital spending and working capital, a set of three statements, a valuation result with enterprise value, and a cost of capital result.
risks: Lists of different lengths are silently cut short, which can hide missing years. Zero depreciation years cause a divide-by-zero error. A WACC that is not above terminal growth gives a meaningless value. The balance sheet is not checked to balance. Tax is never credited on losses. Debt is never repaid. Free cash flow starts from net income after interest, which shifts it toward an equity-based figure.
debug: Start with the method named in the error traceback. Check that every list of inputs has one value per year. Print the WACC and terminal growth rate and confirm WACC is higher. Set initial debt to zero to see whether interest is causing a surprise. Do not treat the balance sheet as proof of accuracy.
